edits.find: The whole question is one phrase on the VCUG: dilation and blunting of the renal calices. Reflux that reaches only the ureter is mild and usually disappears on its own as the intravesical ureter lengthens with growth; reflux that has already deformed the calices is severe, and severe reflux untreated means recurrent febrile UTIs, bacteria in the parenchyma, an inflammatory response, ischemia, and focal wedges of interstitial fibrosis — renal scarring. Enough of it becomes chronic kidney disease, which in a child announces itself as secondary hypertension, proteinuria, and failure to thrive.

Untreated severe reflux leads to recurrent febrile UTIs (urinary tract infections), bacteria in the parenchyma, an inflammatory response and ischemia. The result is focal wedges of interstitial fibrosis, which is renal scarring. Enough scarring becomes chronic kidney disease. In a child, chronic kidney disease presents as secondary hypertension, proteinuria and failure to thrive.

edits.find: The stem is a lower-tract infection and says so four times: no fever, no vomiting, suprapubic tenderness, no back pain. That single classification does most of the elimination, because the anatomic causes of recurrent paediatric urinary infection — reflux above all — produce recurrent pyelonephritis rather than recurrent cystitis. What is left is a mechanical question about emptying, and the stem answers it explicitly: hard stool in the rectal vault in a child with functional constipation since day care. A chronically loaded rectum dilates, and the dilated rectum compresses the bladder and urethra so the bladder never empties; the residual urine is the culture medium, and E. coli ascends from the perineum into it. The management corollary is the part worth storing — treating the cystitis without treating the constipation guarantees a fourth episode, so long-term laxative therapy is part of the prescription.
